title: Mencius's Mother Cuts the Weaving
text:
When Mencius was a boy, his widowed mother supported the household by weaving. She worked hard to give her son an education.

One day the young Mencius came home from his studies early. His mother was at her loom. She asked him how far he had got with his lessons. He answered casually that he was about where he had been before.

Without a word she took a knife and cut through the cloth on her loom, ruining all the work she had done. Mencius was frightened and asked her why.

She told him that his abandoning his studies was just like her cutting the weaving. A scholar studies to make a name and to gain broad knowledge, so that he can live in peace and stay clear of harm. If he gave up now, he would end up as a servant or a thief, unable to escape trouble. Leaving learning halfway, she said, was like a woman who stops weaving cloth halfway: the family would have nothing to wear or eat.

Mencius was shaken. From then on he studied morning and evening without slacking, and he went on to become one of the greatest Confucian thinkers.
lesson: A dramatic, concrete demonstration can teach what many lectures cannot. Abandoning a commitment halfway often wastes everything already put into it.
source: Liu Xiang, Lienu zhuan (Biographies of Exemplary Women), 1.11
caveat: The story was recorded by Liu Xiang in the 1st century BC, centuries after Mencius, and is best treated as a traditional anecdote.
